title: Ultra-Processed Foods in Childhood Linked to Insulin Resistance and Prediabetes Risk
excerpt: A growing body of research shows that diets heavy in packaged snacks, sugary drinks, and fast food during childhood and young adulthood can disrupt blood sugar regulation and increase the risk of type 2 diabetes, with implications for Indian diaspora families navigating food environments in the West.
body:
• A USC longitudinal study found that a 10% increase in ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption among young adults was associated with a 64% higher risk of prediabetes and a 56% higher risk of impaired glucose regulation.
  • In children with obesity, UPF intake was linked to a 30% higher odds of insulin resistance and a 37% increase in odds of moderate-to-severe liver disease (MASLD), according to a Korean study of 149 participants aged 8–17.
  • US children now derive up to 67% of their daily calories from ultra-processed foods, with toddlers at 47% and school-aged children at 59.4%, according to a comprehensive review in Obesity Pillars.

The Evidence Mounts

Multiple studies published over the past year have sharpened the link between ultra-processed food consumption in childhood and metabolic disruption, particularly around insulin response and blood sugar regulation. The findings paint a picture that goes beyond weight gain: even before obesity sets in, the industrial additives, refined sugars, and unhealthy fats in packaged foods appear to rewire how young bodies handle glucose.

The most striking evidence comes from a longitudinal study led by researchers at the Keck School of Medicine at the University of Southern California, published in Nutrition and Metabolism in November 2025. The study tracked 85 young adults aged 17 to 22 — all with a history of overweight or obesity — over four years through the Metabolic and Asthma Incidence Research (Meta-AIR) study. Participants completed dietary recalls and oral glucose tolerance tests at baseline and follow-up.

"Even modest increases in ultra-processed food intake can disrupt glucose regulation in young adults at risk for obesity. These results point to diet as a modifiable driver of early metabolic disease."

— Dr. Vaia Lida Chatzi, Professor of Population and Public Health Sciences, Keck School of Medicine, USC

The results were stark: a 10-percentage-point increase in UPF consumption between visits was associated with 51% higher odds of prediabetes and 158% higher odds of impaired glucose tolerance. Those who ate more UPFs at baseline also showed elevated insulin levels at follow-up — an early marker of insulin resistance, where the body must produce more insulin to maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

Children Bear the Brunt

The problem begins even earlier than young adulthood. A study published in Nutrients examined 149 children and adolescents aged 8 to 17 with obesity in South Korea. Researchers found that those in the highest tertile of UPF consumption had significantly higher insulin levels and insulin resistance. A 10% increase in UPF intake was associated with 30% higher odds of developing insulin resistance and a 37% increase in the odds of moderate-to-severe metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).

A comprehensive review published in Obesity Pillars in September 2025 brought together data from observational studies, systematic reviews, and US policy reports including NHANES data and the 2025 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee's findings. The review found that UPF intake has "dramatically increased during early childhood," with toddlers deriving 47% and school-aged children 59.4% of their daily calories from ultra-processed foods. Higher consumption was linked to pediatric obesity, cardiometabolic risk, mental health concerns, and gut microbiome disruption.

A systematic review published in Nutrients in April 2026 further confirmed a plausible relationship between UPF-rich diets, systemic inflammation, and metabolic dysfunction in pediatric populations, though the authors noted that direct evidence using the NOVA food classification system remained limited.

Why Ultra-Processed Foods Disrupt Metabolism

Ultra-processed foods — defined under the NOVA classification as industrial formulations made with ingredients like hydrogenated oils, high-fructose corn syrup, emulsifiers, and artificial flavors — are engineered for palatability, shelf stability, and low cost. They are calorie-dense but nutrient-poor, typically high in added sugars, sodium, and unhealthy fats while low in fiber, protein, and essential vitamins.

The metabolic damage appears to operate through multiple pathways. The high refined sugar and trans-fat content, combined with low fiber, can cause rapid blood glucose spikes followed by exaggerated insulin responses. Over time, this pattern can lead to insulin resistance — where cells become less responsive to insulin — and eventually prediabetes. Industrial additives may independently contribute to systemic inflammation and gut microbiome disruption, compounding the metabolic harm.

"These findings indicate that ultra-processed food consumption increases the risk for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes among young adults — and that limiting consumption of those foods can help prevent disease."

— Yiping Li, Doctoral Student in Quantitative Biomedical Sciences, Dartmouth College

The Diaspora Dimension

For Indian diaspora families, the findings carry particular urgency. South Asians are already at elevated genetic risk for type 2 diabetes and tend to develop insulin resistance at lower body weights than other populations. Children of Indian origin growing up in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia are immersed in food environments where ultra-processed foods dominate — from school cafeterias to after-school snacks to fast-food culture.

India itself is not immune. The market for packaged and processed foods has expanded rapidly in urban India, with children increasingly consuming branded snacks, sugary beverages, and instant noodles. A 2024 study noted that Asia has seen a sharp rise in UPF consumption among children, raising concerns about the early development of metabolic and cardiovascular conditions in the region.

Pediatricians and nutrition experts are now urging clinicians to screen for UPF consumption during well-child visits. Strategies recommended in the Obesity Pillars review include restricting food marketing to children, implementing clearer front-of-package labeling, improving school meal standards, and providing family-centered dietary counseling.

What Comes Next

Researchers at USC plan to continue investigating the biological mechanisms behind the UPF-diabetes link, including how specific nutrients and additives influence insulin signaling. Future studies with larger cohorts and more granular dietary tracking are needed to identify which specific ultra-processed foods carry the greatest metabolic risk.

A Brazilian randomized controlled trial published in Clinical Obesity in January 2025 offered a note of hope: among 95 children with obesity aged 7 to 12, reducing UPF consumption led to a linear decrease in blood glucose levels of 2.25 mg/dL — independent of BMI changes. The finding suggests that dietary intervention, even without weight loss, can improve metabolic outcomes.

The growing consensus is clear: ultra-processed foods are not just contributing to obesity but are actively disrupting how young bodies regulate blood sugar. For families in the Indian diaspora and beyond, reducing packaged food intake and shifting toward minimally processed diets may be among the most impactful steps for protecting children's long-term metabolic health.
